newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. said threatening Colombia's stability.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said threatening Colombia's stability.

text.p: The United States threatens to undermine Colombia's democratic stability -- and hurt the fight against drugs -- through its public broadsides against President Ernesto Samper, a senior government official said.
The official, Justice Minister Carlos Medellin, issued the warning in a letter to the Washington Post that was made public in Bogota on Thursday.

The letter was written in response to a hard-hitting editorial the U.S. daily ran on Tuesday, in which it derided Colombian anti-drug efforts as a joke because of Samper's alleged ties to Cali cartel kingpins.

The editorial, reprinted under banner headlines in Colombian newspapers, was prompted by a Colombian judge's decision last Friday to give lenient prison sentences to brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the Cali cartel's maximum leaders.

The sentences, which the government has appealed, were handed down under terms of the elaborate plea bargaining arrangements for drug lords that became law under Samper's predecessor Cesar Gaviria, now secretary-general of the Organisation of American States.

In his letter, Medellin noted that members of the administration of U.S. President Bill Clinton have often heaped praise on Colombia's police and military at the same time they were lambasting Samper, the country's commander-in-chief.
"Such tactics serve only to create instability in a democratically elected government and make efforts to cooperate in the drug war more difficult," Medellin said.

He did not elaborate on the threat to stability. But citing what he called "the long and often tragic history between the United States and Latin America," he stressed the importance of "mutual respect for Colombia's democratic institutions."

Samper was cleared by an overwhelming majority in the lower house of Colombia's Congress last June of charges he received millions of dollars in Cali cartel drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign.

U.S. officials dismissed the congressional ruling as a whitewash at the time, and suggested Samper was firmly in the pocket of drug lords. But Medellin said no other Colombian leader had shown as much commitment as Samper to the fight against the drug trade.
"It may be popular politically in Washington to create the impression that the United States is 'working around' President Samper in its drug war efforts in Colombia," he said.
"But those of us on the front line of that war know the truth of the situation: that President Samper's leadership in this struggle has not and will not falter."
